abstract: Empathy requires the ability to generate shared representations of the self and others while maintaining a distinction between them. However, it remains unclear whether, and to what extent, the neural processes involved in sharing and understanding others' pain overlap with those involved in processing one's own pain, particularly with respect to their temporal dynamics. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying empathic processing of self- and other-related painful facial expressions. To this end, EEG signals were recorded from 42 female participants while they viewed self- and other-related painful and neutral expressions. During the early stage of processing, the difference in N2 amplitude between self-related and other-related stimuli was smaller in the painful than in the neutral condition. Nevertheless, self-related painful stimuli continued to elicit more negative N2 amplitudes and greater Alpha/Mu suppression than other-related painful stimuli. In contrast, during the late stage of empathic processing, no distinction was observed between self- and other-related painful stimuli. Instead, painful expressions, regardless of whether they were self- or other-related, elicited larger late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes. These findings suggest that empathic processing is characterized by an early self-other distinction followed by a later convergence in the neural representation of self- and other-related pain.
